name: paralogs

H1.mechanism: ATP6V0E1 and ATP6V0E2 are paralogous c-ring/proteolipid subunits of the V-ATPase V0 domain. Cells that lost ATP6V0E2 expression rely on ATP6V0E1 for lysosomal/endosomal proton pumping; ATP6V0E1 loss is therefore selectively lethal in ATP6V0E2-low cells (paralog buffering).

H2.mechanism: ATP6V0A1 (a1) and ATP6V0A2 (a2) are paralogous V0-a subunit isoforms governing V-ATPase localization. Loss of a1 expression makes cells depend on a2 for V-ATPase function, which is a paralog buffering synthetic lethality.

H3.mechanism: DMXL1 and DMXL2 are paralogous WD40/rabconnectin-3 components of the rabconnectin-3 complex that regulates V-ATPase assembly and endosomal acidification. DMXL2 loss may make cells depend on DMXL1 for V-ATPase function.

findings.claim: Lines with LOSS of ATP6V0E2 (V0 proton-pump c-ring paralog) depend strongly on ATP6V0E1; held-out Broad beta -0.90 (p=1e-29, 18 altered) and Sanger beta -0.88 (p=8e-26, 11 altered). Discovery effect was not confined to one lineage (esophagus/stomach and head-and-neck within-lineage effects both ~-0.9), though ATP6V0E1 is a V-ATPase core subunit and the 'other lines' mean effect is -0.2, so the therapeutic window needs checking.

LOSS of ATP6V0A1 predicted dependence on ATP6V0A2 in discovery (t=-15.8) and held-out Broad lines (beta -0.65, p=3e-12, only 4 altered lines), but the discovery signal was dominated by lymphoid/B-cell and prostate/myeloid lines, and Sanger had zero altered lines so the test could not be run. Not confirmed as a general selective dependency.

LOSS of DMXL2 predicts dependence on DMXL1 (held-out Broad beta -0.57, p=8e-15; Sanger beta -0.58, p=2e-9), consistent with rabconnectin-3 paralog buffering of V-ATPase regulation. Caveats: lymphoid/myeloid-enriched in discovery, and only 3 altered lines in Sanger, so the replication is statistically weak.

summary: I surveyed LOSS_/MUT_ biomarker→dependency pairs and prioritized paralog-type pairs. Three hypotheses were pre-registered and tested. H1 (LOSS_ATP6V0E2 → ATP6V0E1) replicated in both held-out Broad and independent Sanger screens and has no literature hits, making it the strongest novel candidate. H3 (LOSS_DMXL2 → DMXL1) also replicated, though with few Sanger altered lines and partial prior literature on DMXL1–V-ATPase. H2 (LOSS_ATP6V0A1 → ATP6V0A2) did not replicate: its Sanger test was impossible because no lines carried the loss, and the discovery signal was driven largely by lymphoid lines. Caveats: the V-ATPase targets are broadly important, so selectivity windows are uncertain. I did not test RPP25→RPP25L, which has a published paralog-interaction study (PMID 35417719), so it is not novel. Two replication calls remain unused.

Cell lines that have lost NABP1 (hSSB2), enriched in neuroblastoma and embryonal tumours, depend more on its paralog NABP2 (hSSB1); replicated in held-out Broad (p=2e-12) and Sanger (p=3e-7) screens, with a smaller effect in Sanger.

Cell lines that have lost CHPT1 depend more on CEPT1 for the last step of phosphatidylcholine synthesis; replicated (held-out Broad p=5e-6, Sanger p=3e-7), but CEPT1 is also moderately needed in unaltered lines, so the window is narrower.

Cell lines that have lost STK39 (SPAK) depend on OXSR1 (OSR1). This replicated strongly in held-out Broad lines (p=6e-35), but Sanger had too few altered lines (2) to test, so it fails the pre-set criterion.

summary: I surveyed lineage-adjusted LOSS_ and MUT_ biomarker→dependency pairs and picked paralog pairs that held up across lineages. Well-known pairs (RPP25/RPP25L, SMARCA4/SMARCA2, ARID1A/ARID1B) were skipped on purpose. I registered five hypotheses. Four replicated (one-sided p < 0.01 in both held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens): DMXL2→DMXL1, ATP6V0E2→ATP6V0E1, NABP1→NABP2 and CHPT1→CEPT1. STK39→OXSR1 replicated strongly in held-out Broad lines but could not be tested in Sanger (only 2 altered lines), so it does not meet the criterion. Caveats: altered-line counts are small for DMXL2 (5 held-out Broad, 3 Sanger) and CHPT1 (6 held-out Broad, 3 Sanger). DMXL2 and STK39 loss are enriched in blood cancers, and NABP1 loss in neuroblastoma and other neural tumours. CEPT1 is already needed by many unaltered lines, so its therapeutic window is narrower. Novelty is based on PubMed searches that found no paper on these specific pairs. Large published paralog screens may already contain some of them, so "not found" means no dedicated report, not proven novelty.

Cells then rely more on the remaining PRMT5 activity, which requires its obligate partner WDR77 (MEP50) for substrate recognition and methyltransferase activity. MTAP-deleted lines should therefore be more sensitive to WDR77 knockout than MTAP-intact lines.

H2_PRMT5.mechanism: MTA accumulates in MTAP-deleted cells and partially inhibits PRMT5, so these cells depend more on residual PRMT5 methyltransferase activity for splicing (symmetric dimethylation of spliceosomal Sm proteins). Knockout should be more toxic in MTAP-deleted lines.

summary: Across 618 discovery lines, 123 carry LOSS_MTAP. The most selective dependency is WDR77 (the PRMT5 complex partner), with the largest lineage-adjusted effect (beta -0.40, t -8.2). PRMT5 is second (beta -0.24, t -6.1), and MAT2A also appears in the list, consistent with the MTA–PRMT5 axis. Both WDR77 and PRMT5 replicated in held-out Broad lines and in independent Sanger screens (all p < 0.01). WDR77 is ranked first on the data, but PRMT5 is the well-established and clinically validated target (MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors such as MRTX1719 and BMS-986504), so the two should be considered together. Both are broadly essential, so selectivity is modest (mean effect -1.77 vs -1.36 for WDR77) and the therapeutic window is relative rather than absolute. Associations are not driven by a single lineage, though CNS and lymphoid lines contribute strongly.

Budget remaining: 3 replications, unused. Net result: one replicated dependency, which is only partly novel, and one unresolved candidate that is novel but not validated across screens.

summary:
I searched for paralog synthetic-lethal dependencies using LOSS_ and MUT_ biomarkers. I registered two candidates and neither replicated, so this session produced no validated finding.

Part of the plan could not be done. The Python sandbox failed every time with a missing data file, so I could not run a systematic test of all paralog pairs. Instead I tested about 30 candidate pairs one at a time with the scan and inspect tools.

- **Genome-wide top hits are not useful here.** The strongest LOSS and MUT hits (e.g. LOSS_ANXA4 or LOSS_JUN → PAX5, IRF4, HERPUD1, EBF1) come from B-cell and myeloid subtypes inside the lymphoid and myeloid lineages, not from paralog biology.
- **Well-known paralog pairs did not show up in the discovery lines.** This held for MUT_SMARCA4 → SMARCA2, MUT_ARID1A → ARID1B, MUT_STAG2 → STAG1, LOSS_SMARCA2 → SMARCA4 and LOSS_RPP25 → RPP25L, all with p > 0.15. The likely reason is that these biomarkers lump heterozygous changes or passenger loss with true loss, which dilutes the signal.
- **Other plausible pairs were also null:** NMT2/NMT1, CHMP4C/CHMP4B, AP1M2/AP1M1, GNA11/GNAQ, MACROH2A2/MACROH2A1, PRKCZ/PRKCI, SLC25A4/SLC25A5, SYNJ2/SYNJ1, FERMT2/FERMT1, UBE2L6/UBE2L3, EHD2/EHD1, EHD4/EHD1, NUMBL/NUMB, ARHGEF12/ARHGEF11, RAB4A/RAB4B and VANGL1/VANGL2.

**The two registered hypotheses:**
- **H1: MAPK12 loss → MAPK14 dependency.** Discovery evidence was p = 0.002 with 12 altered lines, and the effect held when any single lineage was left out. It did not replicate: p = 0.29 in held-out Broad lines and p = 0.24 in Sanger screens.
- **H2: LDHB loss → LDHA dependency.** Discovery evidence was p = 0.01 with 13 altered lines. It did not replicate: p = 0.32 in held-out Broad lines and p = 0.91 in Sanger screens, where the effect went the wrong way.

Both discovery signals were modest and based on few altered lines, so the replication failures most likely mean they were false positives. I used 2 of the 5 replications and left the other 3 unused. None of the remaining candidates had discovery evidence strong enough to justify registering.

summary: I searched for selective dependencies created by tumor-suppressor loss or other loss-of-function alterations, leaving out paralog pairs. None of the five hypotheses I registered and tested replicated. Notes on the survey: (1) Most of the strongest LOSS/MUT hits genome-wide were markers of a disease subtype rather than of the alteration itself. Many were blood-cancer subtype markers, e.g. MPL, MEF2C, FLT3, POU2AF1, CSK and LRP8 hits in lymphoid/myeloid lines. Others likely reflected lineage or mutation burden: the MYH14, JUP and POU2AF3 hits that recur across many MUT biomarkers, and CIC→TRADD, which was driven by lymphoid lines. (2) Classic tumor suppressors gave weak signals after lineage adjustment, with no FDR-significant non-essential hits. Tested: KEAP1, ARID1A, PTEN, STK11, NF1, NF2, FBXW7, RB1, SMARCA4, SMAD4, BAP1, PBRM1, KMT2D, EP300, APC and RNF43 mutations, plus LOSS_CDKN2A and LOSS_MTAP. (3) I registered five candidates with no prior literature found. Each held across lineages in discovery, but all failed in both held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens, so they were most likely false positives from small altered groups (n=11–22) and the very large number of tests. One choice was weak in hindsight: CDKN2A→UNC45A rested on a large group but a tiny effect. The honest conclusion is that this dataset gave no reproducible, non-paralog loss-of-function dependency from my candidates. The discovery-only signals should be treated as noise.

The effect holds within lung and biliary tract cancers, and when any single lineage is left out. SMARCA2 is not essential in most cells, so there should be a therapeutic window. summary: For PIK3CA hotspot-mutant lines, the clear top selective dependency is PIK3CA itself (oncogene addiction). In the discovery set, the effect was adjusted for lineage, and it held up in every lineage examined and when any one lineage was left out. It replicated strongly in held-out Broad lines (p=4e-13) and in Sanger screens (p=3e-24). This is well established and matches clinical use of alpelisib and inavolisib, the drugs that block mutant p110alpha. AKT1 was a weaker downstream candidate. It passed the threshold in Sanger screens (p=0.0014) but not in held-out Broad lines (p=0.044), so it did not replicate. No new partner gene other than PIK3CA came close to significance after correcting for multiple testing.

H1_RPP25loss_RPP25L.mechanism: Paralog buffering: RPP25 and RPP25L are redundant Alba-family subunits of RNase P/MRP (partnering POP7/RPP20). With RPP25 silenced, RNase P/MRP function relies entirely on RPP25L, so its loss is lethal.

findings.claim: Cancer cells that have lost RPP25 expression depend selectively on its paralog RPP25L, a part of the RNase P/MRP complex, and this held in discovery, held-out Broad and Sanger screens.

summary: RPP25L is the strongest and most selective dependency in cell lines that have lost RPP25 expression, and it replicated. In the discovery lines, lineage-adjusted beta was -0.73 (t=-23.9). 134 of 141 lines with RPP25 loss were strongly dependent on RPP25L (gene effect < -0.5), against 67 of 477 other lines. The effect held within every lineage and when each lineage was left out in turn, and RPP25L is not broadly essential. It replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=2e-59) and in independent Sanger screens (p=3e-25). The likely reason is paralog buffering: RPP25 and RPP25L are interchangeable parts of the RNase P/MRP complex, so cells without RPP25 rely on RPP25L. A 2022 large-scale paralog-screen paper (PMID 35417719) has already reported this pair, so it is partially known rather than new. POP7, the second hit, is broadly essential, so it offers a poorer therapeutic window and I did not test it.

name: HOT_KRAS

H1_KRAS.mechanism: Oncogene addiction: KRAS hotspot-mutant lines depend on the mutant KRAS allele for MAPK/PI3K signalling; all 84 altered lines strongly dependent, consistent across lineages.

H2_RAF1.mechanism: Mutant KRAS signals preferentially through CRAF (RAF1) dimers; CRAF ablation is selectively toxic in KRAS-mutant tumours (non-lung lineages strongest in data).

findings.claim: KRAS hotspot-mutant cancer lines are far more dependent on KRAS itself than other lines are (oncogene addiction), consistently across lineages and in both Broad held-out and Sanger screens.
KRAS hotspot-mutant lines depend selectively on RAF1/CRAF, a non-broadly-essential effector; the effect is modest and absent in lung lines.

summary: For KRAS-hotspot cancers, the strongest and most selective dependency is KRAS itself: oncogene addiction. All 84 of 84 altered discovery lines are strongly dependent on it, the effect holds in every lineage, and it replicated strongly in held-out Broad lines and in Sanger screens (effect about -1.2). The catch is that KRAS is flagged as broadly essential (320 of 542 non-mutant lines also fall below -0.5), so mutant-selective inhibitors (e.g. G12C/G12D-specific drugs) are needed to get a therapeutic window. The best non-self, non-essential candidate is RAF1/CRAF. It replicated in both datasets but with a smaller effect (about -0.25; -0.13 in Sanger), driven by pancreas, bowel and biliary lines and absent in lung. Both findings are already well established in the literature.
